title: Combination Sum
description: Find every unique combination of candidates (with unlimited reuse) that sums to a target value.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given an array of distinct positive integers candidates and a target integer target, return every unique combination of numbers from candidates that sums exactly to target. The same number may be chosen an unlimited number of times. Combinations are considered different only if the chosen multiset of numbers differs; order within a combination does not matter.

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Pattern","Backtracking over choices, with unlimited reuse of each candidate (unbounded knapsack style combination search)."],["Difficulty","Medium"],["Tags","Recursion, Backtracking, Array"],["Interview Focus","Recognizing when reuse is allowed the recursive call must NOT advance past the current index, and using sorting to prune entire branches early instead of just checking after the fact."]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

blocks.title: Analogy: An Unlimited Coin Jar
blocks.text: Picture a jar holding coins of denominations 2, 3, 6, and 7, with an unlimited supply of each. You want every distinct way to pick coins (in any quantity, repeats allowed) so they add up to exactly 7. You could pick 2+2+3, or just a single 7 coin. You never pick the same MULTISET of coins twice, but you are free to reuse any single denomination as many times as you like within one attempt.

blocks.caption: Picking reusable coins until the running total hits the target exactly

blocks.text: The key twist that separates this from a plain subset-sum problem is reuse: once you decide to use the value 2, you are still allowed to use another 2 right after it. This means the search space is not "include or exclude each element once" but "how many times, if any, should each element be used."
4. Understand with Examples
Example 1

Input: candidates = [2, 3, 6, 7], target = 7
Output: [[2, 2, 3], [7]]

blocks.text: Example 2: candidates = [2, 3, 5], target = 8 gives [[2, 2, 2, 2], [2, 3, 3], [3, 5]]. Every combination is reachable by the same reuse-and-backtrack process, just with a different set of coin denominations.
5. How Should We Think?
Before writing any code, it helps to reason through the shape of the problem out loud, the way an interviewer wants to see.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text: Observation 1: Since numbers can repeat, this is not a simple "include or exclude" decision per element like a classic subset problem, it is "how many times does each element get used, if at all." Observation 2: A recursive/backtracking exploration naturally models this, if a call is allowed to pick the SAME index again on its next recursive step, reuse falls out for free. Observation 3: To avoid ever generating the same combination twice in a different order, each recursive call must only consider candidates at the CURRENT index or later, never earlier ones, that way [2, 3] is only ever built as 2-then-3, never as 3-then-2. Observation 4: Every path that overshoots the target is useless and can be abandoned early, if the candidates are sorted, the moment one candidate is too large, every candidate after it is too large as well, so the entire remaining loop can be skipped, not just the current pick. Punchline: sort the candidates once, then backtrack index-by-index-or-later, staying on the same index to allow reuse, and stop scanning a level the instant a candidate exceeds what is left to reach the target.

This reasoning naturally splits into a brute-force version (backtrack without the sorting-based early exit) and an optimized version (sort first, then prune entire branches early) -- both explored below.
6. Brute Force Solution

The most direct approach is to backtrack over every candidate at every position, staying on the same index whenever a number is picked (to allow reuse) and moving to the next index whenever a number is skipped. A combination is recorded whenever the remaining target hits exactly 0, and a branch is abandoned once the remaining target goes negative.
Why the code is written this way

items: The recursive call passes the SAME start index (not start + 1) after picking a candidate, which is exactly what allows that candidate to be reused in the very next step.
The base case checks remaining === 0 (record) BEFORE checking remaining < 0 (abandon), since a path can only ever be in one of these two states once it stops being strictly positive.
The shared current list is appended to right before the recursive call and popped right after it returns, so every sibling branch sees a clean list with no leftover values from an earlier attempt.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text: Time Complexity: roughly O(2^target) in the worst case (the exact bound depends on candidate values and count, but grows exponentially with the target since every candidate can be picked repeatedly at every depth). Space Complexity: O(target / minCandidate) for the recursion depth, plus O(number of combinations) to store the results.

This works correctly, but every recursive call scans candidates starting from position 0 upward without ever short-circuiting early, even when it is already obvious (because the list happens to be unsorted, or simply because no check was added) that no candidate from a certain point onward could possibly fit. On instances with many candidates larger than the remaining target, this wastes real work checking candidates that were always going to fail the remaining < 0 base case one level deeper.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Why does the brute force waste work? Because it only discovers a candidate does not fit AFTER recursing one level deeper and hitting the remaining < 0 base case, one wasted function call per oversized candidate. What is the bottleneck? Checking every candidate at every position regardless of whether it could possibly still fit. Can we avoid the bottleneck? Yes, if the candidates are sorted ascending, then the moment one candidate exceeds the remaining target, every candidate after it (being even larger) is guaranteed to exceed it too. Can we combine this with anything already known? This is the same "sorted order turns a per-item check into a whole-range skip" idea used by problems like 3Sum and Search a 2D Matrix II. The core idea: sort candidates once up front, then break out of the loop entirely (not just skip one candidate) the instant candidates[i] > remaining.
This single change, replacing an eventual deep recursive rejection with an immediate loop break, prunes away entire subtrees of guaranteed-failing recursive calls before they are ever started.
9. Optimized Solution

Sort the candidates once at the start. During backtracking, the moment the current candidate is larger than what remains, break out of the loop immediately, since every later candidate (sorted ascending) is at least as large and would also fail.

blocks.caption: Same input/output shape, now reached by pruning entire branches early

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text: Time Complexity: still exponential in the worst case, but with a much smaller constant factor in practice since entire branches are pruned the instant a candidate overshoots, instead of being explored one wasted level deeper. Space Complexity: O(target / minCandidate) recursion depth, same as the brute force, plus O(number of combinations) for the results, plus O(n log n) for the one-time sort.
Why This Works
Sorting does not change which combinations are valid, it only changes the ORDER candidates are visited in, and that order is exactly what makes an early break safe.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Candidate vs Remaining","What It Means","What The Code Does"],"rows":[["candidate <= remaining","This candidate can still be part of a valid combination.","Pick it, recurse with the same index, then undo the pick."],["candidate > remaining (sorted list)","This candidate, and every candidate after it, is too large.","Break out of the loop entirely instead of continuing to the next index."]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: Sorting happens exactly once, outside the recursive helper, so its O(n log n) cost is never repeated across recursive calls.

The loop condition changed from a deep "remaining < 0" rejection to a shallow "candidates[i] > remaining" check performed BEFORE recursing at all, which is what turns a wasted function call into a simple break.
Everything else (same-index reuse, append-recurse-pop pattern) stays identical to the brute force, since the correctness logic did not change, only how early a hopeless branch is abandoned.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Combination Sum is a foundational backtracking-with-reuse problem. The two ideas to walk away with: staying on the same index enables unlimited reuse, and sorting first turns a deep rejection into a shallow, whole-branch skip.
Common Mistakes

items: Advancing the recursive call to start + 1 after picking a candidate, which silently disables reuse and produces wrong (incomplete) results.
Forgetting to pop the just-tried candidate off the shared path after the recursive call returns, which corrupts every sibling branch explored afterward.
Using break instead of continue on an unsorted candidates array, which would incorrectly skip candidates that might still have fit, since sortedness is what makes break safe in the first place.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["No combination sums to target","Return an empty list, not null or an error."],["A single candidate exactly equals target","That candidate alone forms a valid one-element combination."],["target is smaller than every candidate","No combination is possible; the very first loop iteration already breaks immediately."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tip: If asked to also forbid reuse (each candidate usable at most once), the fix is a one-line change: recurse with start + 1 instead of start, turning this into the closely related Combination Sum II pattern.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "numbers can be used more than once", think: recurse with the SAME index. If they say "avoid duplicate combinations in the output", think: always advance the starting index forward, never backward, so a set of values is only ever discovered in one order.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would the solution change if each candidate could only be used once?
How would you count just the NUMBER of valid combinations, without listing them, and would that let you use dynamic programming instead?
What if the candidates array could contain duplicate values, how would you avoid duplicate combinations in the output?
How does the time complexity change as target grows versus as the candidates array grows?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Generate Parentheses: same backtrack-with-a-shared-mutable-buffer shape, different branching rule.
Subsets and Permutations: same family of index-driven backtracking, but without the "stay on the same index" reuse rule.
3Sum and Search a 2D Matrix II: same "sort first, then use monotonic order to skip whole ranges early" pruning idea.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute Force: O(2^target) time, O(target/minCandidate) space. Optimized: same exponential worst case but far fewer wasted calls in practice, thanks to sorting + early break.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Backtracking with unlimited reuse of each choice.
Core Idea: Recurse while staying on the same index to allow reuse, advance the index to avoid duplicate combinations.
Time: O(2^target) worst case, reduced constant factor after sorting + pruning.
Space: O(target / minCandidate) recursion depth plus the output itself.
Most Important Observation: Sorting turns "this candidate does not fit" into "no candidate from here on fits", replacing many individual rejections with one loop break.
Interview Difficulty: Medium, a standard backtracking template every candidate should be fluent in.
One-line memory trick: "Same index to reuse, sort to prune."
